questions.stem: Describe the weighted decision matrix.
options: Criteria with weights, each option scored on each criterion, weighted scores totalled
A list of pros and cons
questions.why: Visible, arguable and repeatable — which is what defensible means. See §9.1.

questions.stem: Identify the rule that makes the matrix honest.
options: Set the criteria and the weights before you look at the options
Let the boss choose the weights
Change the weights until the favourite wins
questions.why: Weights chosen afterwards are your preference wearing a table. See §9.1.

questions.stem: Explain what to do if the matrix winner surprises you.
options: Do not adjust the weights — ask what the matrix knows that your instinct did not
questions.why: Ask what the matrix knows. See §9.1.

questions.stem: Identify the winning option in the chapter's example matrix.
Describe how a weighted score is calculated.
options: Score times weight — a score of 4 on a weight-5 criterion gives 20

questions.stem: Identify the formula for sizing a risk.
options: Threat = probability × seriousness, scoring high, medium and low as 3, 2 and 1
questions.why: Kepner-Tregoe potential problem analysis in its simplest form. See §9.2.

questions.stem: Identify the threat score that requires a written contingency.
questions.why: Below 6, name it and move on. See §9.2.

questions.stem: Describe the contingency for 'staff do not use the new process' in the chapter's table.
options: Train and pilot on one counter first
questions.why: High × high = 9 → contingency. See §9.2.

questions.stem: Explain why listing risks is not enough.
options: You must size them and do something about the biggest two
questions.why: Size them, then act on the biggest. See §9.2.

questions.stem: Identify the threat score for a medium-probability, high-seriousness risk.
Describe a second-order effect.
options: An effect the decision produces that it did not intend
questions.why: Every decision produces effects it did not intend. See §9.3.

questions.stem: Identify the question that finds second-order effects.
questions.why: Ask it twice of every recommendation. See §9.3.

questions.stem: Identify the second-order effect of an express lane for simple orders.
options: Complex orders wait longer — and those customers spend most
questions.why: The second answer is where the cost hides. See §9.3.

questions.stem: Identify the second-order effect of a bonus per order processed.
options: Staff avoid the difficult orders and quality falls
questions.why: The first answer is the hoped-for benefit. See §9.3.

questions.stem: Explain why the second 'and then what?' matters most.
options: The first answer is the hoped-for benefit; the second is where the cost usually hides
The first answer is always wrong
questions.why: It is what a good manager will ask you about. See §9.3.

questions.stem: Identify the four questions of the ethical screen.
options: Who bears the cost? The public test. The reversal test. The precedent test.
Is it legal? Is it cheap? Is it fast? Is it popular?
questions.why: Four minutes, four questions. See §9.4.

questions.stem: Describe the reversal test.
options: Would you accept this if you were on the receiving end?
Would you be comfortable if it were reported?
If everyone did this, would it be acceptable?
questions.why: The reversal test. See §9.4.

questions.stem: Describe the precedent test.
options: If everyone in the industry did this, would the outcome still be acceptable?
questions.why: The precedent test. See §9.4.

questions.stem: Explain what to do when an ethical test fails.
options: Say so in the report and state what you would do to reduce the harm
questions.why: You are not required to abandon; you are required to say so. See §9.4.

questions.stem: Explain why 'legal and profitable' is not enough.
options: A recommendation can be legal, profitable and still wrong — these are the questions asked when it goes badly in public
questions.why: Legal, profitable and still wrong. See §9.4.

questions.stem: Describe what AI is good for in problem solving.
options: Widening options, suggesting causes, playing the challenger, rewriting for a different reader
questions.why: A thinking partner, not a thinker. See §9.5.

questions.stem: Describe what AI is bad for.
options: Evidence — it produces plausible facts, numbers and sources that do not exist
questions.why: Anything it gives as a fact must be checked. See §9.5.

questions.stem: Describe the Doshi and Hauser (2024) finding.
options: AI raises individual creative output but reduces the collective diversity of ideas
questions.why: Groups using it converge on similar answers. See §9.5.

questions.stem: Identify the course rule on AI.
options: AI may help you think; it may not do the thinking that is assessed — and you declare what you used it for
AI use need not be declared
questions.why: Declare what you used it for. See §9.5.

questions.stem: Explain what to do after AI widens your options.
options: Deliberately go beyond it — groups using AI converge
questions.why: Use it to widen, then go beyond it. See §9.5.

questions.stem: Identify the six parts of the defence in order.
options: Recommendation; the problem with evidence; what was rejected; cost and trade-offs; main risk and contingency; what you are still unsure about
Problem; history; options; recommendation; thanks; questions
Cost; benefit; risk; timeline; team; budget
Claim; reason; assumption; evidence; conclusion; vote
questions.why: Each answers the question the listener is actually asking. See §9.6.

questions.stem: Identify what comes first in the defence.
options: The recommendation — 'what do you want me to do?'
questions.why: The recommendation, first, in 25 words. See §9.6.

questions.stem: Explain why the last line of the defence earns trust.
options: Naming your remaining uncertainty makes everything before it more believable
questions.why: The one students omit. See §9.6.

questions.stem: Identify the question behind 'what else you considered and rejected'.
options: 'What is this going to cost me?'
questions.why: Rejected options show you thought. See §9.6.

questions.stem: Explain why the defence is not salesmanship.
options: It is a structure that answers the questions a manager will actually ask, in order
questions.why: Not salesmanship. See §9.6.

questions.stem: Describe what to do with a risk scoring below 6.
options: Name it and move on — you cannot plan for everything
questions.why: Below 6, name it and move on. See §9.2.

questions.stem: Explain what 'defensible' means for a decision.
options: Visible, arguable and repeatable — someone else could follow how it was reached
questions.why: Visible, arguable, repeatable. See §9.1.

questions.stem: Analyse a group that changes the weights after Option B wins unexpectedly. Determine the verdict.
options: Dishonest — ask what the matrix knows instead of tuning the weights
questions.why: Do not adjust the weights. See §9.1.

questions.stem: Determine the weighted score for a score of 3 on a weight-4 criterion.
Select the correct sequence in the week-12 studio.
options: Agree criteria and weights on the board, witnessed, then score the options
Score the options, then agree the criteria
Let the client set the weights
questions.why: Criteria and weights before any option is scored. See Exercise 1 and §9.1.

questions.stem: Analyse a matrix with one criterion weighted 10 and four weighted 1. Determine the problem.
options: One criterion decides everything — the matrix is a single preference wearing a table
questions.why: Weights must reflect what matters, set before. See §9.1.

questions.stem: Determine the threat score and action for 'supplier cannot deliver in time' (medium, high).
options: 6 — write a contingency such as naming a second supplier
questions.why: 2 × 3 = 6 → contingency. See §9.2.

questions.stem: Determine the action for 'system integration fails' scored 3 (low, high).
options: Name it and ask IT to confirm before signing — no written contingency required
questions.why: Below 6: name and move on. See §9.2.

questions.stem: Analyse a report that lists ten risks and acts on none. Determine the fault.
options: Risks were not sized, so nothing was done about the biggest
questions.why: Size them, then act on the biggest two. See §9.2.

questions.stem: Select the contingency for 'customers dislike the change' scored 4.
options: Name it; optionally test with 20 customers and keep the old option
questions.why: Score 4 is below 6. See §9.2.

questions.stem: Analyse 'cut opening hours to save cost'. Determine the second-order effect.
options: Regulars shift to a competitor and do not return
questions.why: The second answer hides the cost. See §9.3.

questions.stem: Analyse a bonus for calls handled per hour. Determine the likely second-order effect.
options: Calls get shorter and difficult callers are avoided; quality falls
questions.why: Staff avoid the difficult ones. See §9.3.

questions.stem: Determine the chapter's distinction between a student answer and a professional one.
options: The professional asks 'and then what?' twice and reports the inconvenient second answer
questions.why: Ask it twice, of every recommendation. See §9.3.

questions.stem: Analyse 'add a pre-order shelf'. Determine a possible second-order effect.
options: Counter customers wait longer while staff fill pre-orders
questions.why: And then what? twice. See §9.3.

questions.stem: Analyse a recommendation to cut the night cleaning shift. Determine the group the first ethical question points to.
options: The cleaners who lose hours — with no voice in the meeting
questions.why: Name every group affected, including those with no voice. See §9.4.

questions.stem: Classify 'would we be comfortable if this decision and our reason were reported accurately?'.
questions.why: The public test. See §9.4.

questions.stem: Determine the action when the precedent test fails but the recommendation stands.
options: State the failure in the report and what you would do to reduce the harm
questions.why: Say so, and reduce the harm. See §9.4 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Analyse a recommendation that is legal and raises profit by charging hidden fees. Determine the screen's likely verdict.
options: Fails the public and reversal tests
questions.why: Legal, profitable and still wrong. See §9.4.

questions.stem: Classify using AI to argue against your recommendation.
questions.why: Playing the challenger is a good use. See §9.5 and Exercise 3.

questions.stem: Classify citing three statistics an AI produced, without checking.
options: Bad use — AI invents plausible facts and sources
questions.why: Anything given as a fact must be checked. See §9.5.

questions.stem: Analyse a group whose option list came only from AI. Determine the risk.
options: Convergence — groups using AI produce similar answers; go beyond it deliberately
questions.why: Doshi and Hauser (2024). See §9.5.

questions.stem: Select the correct two-line AI declaration.
options: 'Used AI to widen options and as a challenger; did not use it for the diagnosis, the choice or the defence'
questions.why: What you used it for, and what you did not. See §9.5 and Exercise 3.

questions.stem: Determine how many of three AI-supplied facts a group should expect to survive checking.
options: Unknown until each is verified against a real source — that is the point of the exercise
questions.why: Verify each; report how many survived. See Exercise 3. See §9.5.

questions.stem: Analyse a defence that opens with ten minutes of history. Determine the fault.
options: The recommendation should come first — the listener is asking 'what do you want me to do?'
questions.why: Recommendation first, in 25 words. See §9.6.

questions.stem: Analyse a defence that never mentions what was rejected. Determine the question left unanswered.
options: 'What is this going to cost me?'
questions.why: Rejected options answer that question. See §9.6.

questions.stem: Determine the word budget for the recommendation in the defence.
questions.why: 25 words. See §9.6.

questions.stem: Analyse a defence that ends with 'we are completely certain this will work'. Determine the chapter's view.
options: It loses trust — naming remaining uncertainty makes the rest more believable
questions.why: Naming uncertainty earns trust. See §9.6.

questions.stem: Determine the time limit for the studio defence.
questions.why: Over four minutes is a fail. See Exercise 4. See §9.6.

questions.stem: Select the part that answers 'what happens if it goes wrong?'.
options: The main risk and your contingency
questions.why: Risk and contingency. See §9.6.

questions.stem: Analyse a group whose matrix winner is the option their test in chapter 8 ruled out. Determine the fault.
options: The test result was not used as a criterion or to remove the option
questions.why: A test result feeds the decision. See §9.1 and §8.6.

questions.stem: Determine the ethical question that catches a recommendation harming a group not present.
options: 'Who bears the cost?' — name every group affected, including those with no voice
questions.why: Including the ones with no voice in the meeting. See §9.4.

questions.stem: Analyse 'staff do not use the new process' rated high and high. Determine the score.
Classify the sentence 'what we are still unsure about is whether the effect holds in a full month'.
options: The sixth part of the defence — remaining uncertainty
questions.why: The part students omit. See §9.6.
